subject: Pathology
summary: Arachidonic acid is a key fatty acid that fuels eicosanoid production, driving inflammation, pain, fever, and vascular tone. Its dysregulation underlies many acute and chronic inflammatory conditions.

sections.p: Arachidonic acid (20:4) is a polyunsaturated fatty acid stored in membrane phospholipids. Release by phospholipase A2 during inflammation leads to prostaglandins, leukotrienes, and thromboxanes.
b: Non‑essential but abundant in cell membranes

sections.p: Severity is gauged by the extent of eicosanoid‑mediated inflammation: mild (localized pain), moderate (systemic fever), severe (sepsis, anaphylaxis).
Common triggers include infection, trauma, NSAID use, and allergic reactions. In low‑resource settings, malaria, TB, HIV, and herbal remedies can precipitate excessive AA release.
Patients may have pain, redness, warmth, fever, bronchoconstriction, or platelet aggregation. Systemic signs include tachycardia, hypotension, and respiratory distress.
Lab tests assess downstream eicosanoids and inflammatory status.
b: If tests unavailable, assess clinical signs and response to NSAIDs or steroids

t.b: Increased aggregation points to thromboxane overproduction

sections.p: Rapid progression to shock, severe bronchospasm, or uncontrolled bleeding signals life‑threatening complications.
Treat the inciting cause, then modulate AA pathways. NSAIDs block COX, steroids inhibit PLA2, leukotriene antagonists block LTB4/LTC4 pathways, and antiplatelets reduce thromboxane effects.
b: Corticosteroids – inhibit PLA2, lowering all eicosanoids

t.b: Improvement suggests COX‑mediated prostaglandins were key
Rapid response indicates PLA2‑driven AA release

sections.p: Monitor inflammatory markers, repeat imaging if needed, and counsel on avoiding NSAID overuse and managing underlying infections.
Other inflammatory mediators such as cytokines (IL‑6, TNF‑α) or prostaglandin‑independent pain pathways.
Low prostaglandin levels may occur in chronic steroid use; leukotriene assays can be falsely low if sample is delayed.
b: Delayed sample handling reduces leukotriene detection

faq.q: Why does aspirin cause bronchospasm in some patients?
faq.a: Aspirin blocks COX, shunting AA to the lipoxygenase pathway, increasing leukotrienes that cause bronchoconstriction.

faq.q: Can diet influence arachidonic acid levels?
faq.a: Yes, diets high in omega‑6 fatty acids increase AA availability, while omega‑3 intake can compete and reduce AA‑derived eicosanoids.

faq.q: What is the main difference between prostaglandins and leukotrienes?
faq.a: Prostaglandins are COX products causing vasodilation and pain; leukotrienes are lipoxygenase products that attract neutrophils and cause bronchoconstriction.

exam: Explain how NSAID use can worsen asthma in susceptible patients.
Describe the diagnostic approach to a patient with suspected AA‑mediated sepsis.
Outline the stepwise management of a patient with severe AA‑driven bronchospasm.
